newsitem.title: Guatemala: Guatemala army confronts rebel military police.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala army confronts rebel military police.

text.p: Just one month after a historic peace treaty ended Guatemala's long guerrilla war, troops on Saturday moved on rebellious military police demanding compensation when their jobs disappear, a victim of the peace pact.
No injuries were reported after the brief burst of gunfire on Saturday as army troops and four tanks surrounded a compound held by the military police since Wednesday night.

Ex-president Ramiro de Leon Carpio entered the fortified compound, in a poor residential district of the capital, just after midnight (0600 GMT) but left shortly afterwards saying he was not able to negotiate an end to the confrontation.
He told reporters the negotiation failed because he could not get President Alvaro Arzu on the phone as the military police demanded.
The military police, who are demanding government promises of severance pay said they wanted a peaceful end to the rebellion but maintained armed positions in turrets along the walls of the compound.
The conflict marks the first sign of military discontent over terms of a peace accord signed between the government and leftist rebels in December.
The army has played a pivotal and at times brutal role in political life for much of Guatemala's recent history.
The war claimed an estimated 140,000 lives, many of them poor Indian civilians killed in army counterinsurgency campaigns.

The entire 4,000-member military police force is due to be disbanded this year as part of drastic army cuts the government promised when it signed peace accords Dec. 29 with leftist rebels the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG).

Hundreds of military police rebelled on Wednesday, taking over their own headquarters and refusing to turn in their weapons. They complained that the peace accords did not specify what, if any, compensation they would receive when they lose their jobs and said the URNG guerrillas had won a better deal in the peace accords than the military.
Many of the about 1,000 military police housed in the compound have refused to report to work guarding banks and businesses in the capital during the protest.
A commission of three army generals began negotiating with the military police on Thursday and promised a government response on Saturday.

But when the three generals returned to the compound on Saturday afternoon and asked for more time for the government to come up with concrete terms, the revolt turned ugly and military discipline broke down.
Disgruntled military police carrying assault rifles surrounded the generals, heckling and shoving them. The rebellious police briefly kept all three generals from leaving the compound.
Two of the generals eventally left but one remained inside the fortress and was still a hostage on Saturday night.
